title: Present Fathers, Fatherless Children
author: Anthony B. Bradley
summary: Anthony Bradley introduces a new series on father-child attachment, opening with the claim that shared activity between a father and his kids is not the same as closeness. Drawing on psychoanalyst Susan Schwartz's work on fathers and sons -- including the case of 'Bernard,' whose father attended every game but offered little emotional connection -- Bradley argues that fatherlessness can occur even when a father lives in the home, and previews the attachment-related harms facing sons and daughters who lack secure emotional bonds with their fathers.
points: Challenges the common assumption that attending a child's activities equals closeness, citing psychoanalyst Susan Schwartz's case study of 'Bernard,' a man whose emotionally distant but ever-present father shaped his adult struggles.
Argues fatherlessness is not defined by physical absence alone -- a father can live in the home and still leave children father-deprived without secure attachment.
Cites Britannica's definition of attachment theory to frame why safety, comfort, and emotional regulation from fathers matter developmentally.

Lists the downstream effects of insecure father attachment separately for boys (anxiety, addiction, low self-esteem) and girls (paternal longing, difficulty trusting others, identity struggles), previewing a multi-week series.
quotes: A son whose father attends all of his soccer, baseball, hockey, lacrosse, football, and basketball games, as well as every other sporting event, can still be father-deprived and emotionally fatherless.
Bernard’s father showed up for sports, but affection and personal conversation were almost nonexistent.
Fatherlessness and father deprivation can occur even when a father lives in the home and regularly participates in activities with his children.
When children are securely attached to their fathers, they look to them for safety, comfort, protection, and emotional regulation.

For boys, a lack of secure attachment to their fathers can contribute to anxiety, addiction, low energy, low self-esteem, perfectionism, withdrawal, shame, poor academic performance, and unemployment.
With an evidence-based approach, it seems that we need to rethink everything about how we’re raising kids in the 21st-century at home, school, and church.
